t: four kinds of bailees are mentioned in the Torah and they have three laws. The Torah mentions four types of people who hold another's property and are obligated to guard it, but in terms of their liability for the item in their hands, they divide into three.
an unpaid bailee. Who receives no payment for guarding the deposit and may not use it.
and the borrower. Who received the item in order to use it, and does not pay the lender for this.
a paid bailee. A bailee for hire, who receives payment for guarding the deposit and may not use it.
and the renter. Who pays the owner rent for the use of the item.
was taken captive. Was captured by others.

he swears that he guarded it in the manner of bailees. According to the way of guarding customary for a deposit, for if he was negligent and did not guard it properly he must pay. And he includes in his oath what happened to the deposit that is no longer in his possession, and that he did not lay a hand on it beforehand (see Hilchot She'elah u-Pikadon 4:1-3, 6:1).

as it is said, 'and it is stolen from the man's house'. Earlier it says: 'If a man gives his neighbor money or articles to keep, and it is stolen from the man's house' (Exodus 22:6), and the Sages learned that this passage speaks of an unpaid bailee, who is exempt for theft and loss (Bava Metzia 94b).

and the master of the house shall come near to God. The Sages explained that 'God' here is a term for judges, and that this approach is the oath administered to the bailee about his claim (ibid. 41b).
that died. By an act of Heaven.
was broken. For example it was injured by a wild animal or damaged in another way (see Mekhilta of Rabbi Yishmael and Mekhilta of Rashbi on Exodus 22:9 and the Bible commentators there).
for so it is written regarding the borrower, 'and it is injured or dies'. And the beginning of the verse states explicitly: 'And if a man borrows from his neighbor' (Exodus 22:13).
if its owner is not with him, he shall surely pay. And if its owner is with him, he is exempt, as below, halakhah 3.
or took payment for guarding it. The deposit that he guards for payment.

as it is said, 'and it dies or is injured'. Earlier it says: 'If a man gives his neighbor a donkey, ox, sheep or any animal to keep' (Exodus 22:9), and the Sages learned that this passage speaks of a paid bailee (Bava Metzia 94b). The Sages equated the renter with the paid bailee because in both cases there is benefit both to the one who receives the item and to the owner of the item, and therefore damages are divided between them and the owner.
an oath of the Lord shall be between them. Hence in a case of unavoidable accident he swears and is exempt.

and it says, 'if it is stolen from him, he shall pay its owner; if it is torn by a beast'. Hence he is liable for theft and exempt for unavoidable accident such as being torn by a beast and the like. The Sages derived by a fortiori reasoning that he is liable for loss too, for if he is liable for theft, which has an element of accident, all the more so is he liable for loss, which has an element of negligence (ibid.).
as will be explained. Hilchot She'elah u-Pikadon 1:1.
by an armed robber. An armed bandit.

if the bailee asked the owners along with their item, or hired them. That when he took the item he asked them to do some work for him, or hired them to do so (for the details of this law see Hilchot She'elah u-Pikadon, chapter 2).

if its owner is with him, he shall not pay etc.. If the owner of the item was lent to the bailee or the borrower, the latter need not pay for the loss of the item. [From the fact that Maimonides cited here the end of the verse, 'if he is hired, he came for his hire', it may be that he understood the verse to mean that if the owner of the item was hired by the bailee or borrower ('if he is hired'), he does not pay him for the loss of the item but pays him his wages only ('he came for his hire').]
even though the owners are not with him there. Since they are lent or hired to him, he is exempt, even if they are in another place.
they learned from tradition. The tradition of the Sages in explaining the verses.
for all of them are exempt when the owners are with them. For if the owners were lent or hired to the bailees at the time of the deposit, they are exempt.
any bailee who was negligent at the outset. Who did not guard the deposit properly.
as will be explained. Below 3:9.
he may not rent it to another. He may not rent it to another person (some read 'yaskirenu'; but in Maimonides' writing one finds interchange between the verbs 'sakhar' and 'hiskir' - R. Y. Shilat).
the bailee transgressed. He acted improperly.
and he shall take the matter up with the second bailee. The fact that the depositor received his property does not exempt the second bailee from responsibility toward the first.
even if the first was an unpaid bailee and transferred it to a paid bailee. And the level of responsibility for the deposit rose.
you are trusted by me to swear and this one is not trusted. And since the depositor does not trust the second bailee, the first bailee must pay the depositor.

such as where it was deposited with him for pay and he deposited it with that second one without pay. The first bailee was liable for theft and loss, and the second bailee is exempt for theft and loss.
or where it was borrowed by him and he deposited it with that second one for pay. The first was liable even for unavoidable accident, and the second is exempt.
even if he borrowed or hired together with the owners. And should have been exempt even for negligence (as above, halakhah 3).

for he removed the guarded item from his hand to the hand of another bailee. The exemption of borrowing or hiring together with the owners applies only when the event occurs while the deposit is in the hand of the bailee who borrowed or hired the owner, and not when it occurs after he passed it to another (Maggid Mishneh).
according to the law of his guarding. Of the first.
a paid bailee who gave the animal being guarded to an unpaid bailee. And thereby reduced its guarding.
and the animal died its natural death. And even a paid bailee is exempt in such a case.
the benefit. The profit.
and it died its natural death in the hand of the borrower. And the borrower is liable in this case and the renter is exempt.

the price of the cow shall be returned to the owners. The owners receive the price of the cow from the borrower, and the renter cannot take it from the borrower and keep it on the claim that he is exempt in case of its death.
for this renter is not trading with the other's cow. The cow was rented to him for work only and not beyond that.

since the first bailee is liable for its safekeeping until it reaches the owner's hand. For the owner of the deposit did not make him an agent. But if the owner of the deposit made him an agent to return the deposit to him from the bailee's hand, the bailee is released from responsibility as soon as the deposit is handed to the agent (Hilchot Sheluchin ve-Shutafin 2:3).

if he wishes to retract and return the deposit from the second bailee's hand, he may return it. For as long as the deposit is in the agent's hand and the bailee remains responsible, he can take the deposit back into his hand (unlike a loan, where in any case he cannot retract - see Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 16:2).
a denier. A person who is not trustworthy.
he cannot take back the deposit from the second bailee. For certainly the depositor wants the deposit to remain in the agent's hand, and the agent acquires the deposit on his behalf.
and of an ordinary person. Unconsecrated property.
land is excluded. Land is not movable property and therefore is not included in the laws of bailees.
and slaves, who are equated with land, are excluded. They are equated with land halakhically (see Hilchot Genevah 2:2).
and documents, whose substance is not money, are excluded. For the value of a document is not derived from the value of the paper but from what is written on it.
consecrated items are excluded. Temple property, which is property of the Most High and is not included in 'his neighbor'.
he does not swear. If the deposit was stolen, lost or destroyed by accident, he need not swear that he was not negligent in order to be exempt.
and a paid bailee or renter does not pay. Even if the deposit was stolen or lost, for which in the usual case he is liable, in these matters he is exempt.

but if they made a kinyan, he is liable for their safekeeping. If they agreed that the bailee would be subject to the laws of bailees even for these items, and they made a kinyan sudar to that effect (see Hilchot Mekhirah 5:5 and the commentary there).
and the Sages instituted that the bailee's oath be administered regarding consecrated items. That every bailee must swear in accordance with his law.
like one of the Torah. While holding a Torah scroll (an oath taken while grasping an object), similar to a severe oath of the Torah (see Hilchot Shevu'ot 11:8).

for anyone who is negligent is a damager, and there is no difference between the law of one who damages land and one who damages movables. For what the Torah exempted bailees in these matters is from payments arising from the laws of safekeeping and not from payments arising from causing damage, and for causing damage there is no exemption for land and the like.

and so my teachers ruled. Regarding handing over a vineyard on condition that he work it, that if he was negligent he is liable because he is a direct damager (see R. Yosef Migash, Shevu'ot 42b - though regarding a bailee who was negligent with land and the like, R. Yosef Migash there holds he is exempt, unlike Maimonides' view in the previous passage).
in a tenancy for a share of the crop. The sharecropper works the field for the owner in return for a portion of the produce.
he should dust. Spread dust on the exposed roots of the trees.

even if they were grapes ready to be harvested. Although they do not need the ground, they are considered land for the laws of bailees because he gives him the grapes to guard (but when he gives them to him in order to pick them, if they do not need the ground and are ready for harvest, they are considered movable property - R. Yosef Migash, Shevu'ot 43a; and see Hilchot Mekhirah 1:17, Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 5:4).
and afterward. While it was with the bailee.
he redeemed it. He paid its value to the Temple treasury and took it out to unconsecrated status.
and it was unconsecrated at the time he took it from the bailee's hand. At the time he came to take it from the bailee, and before that an unavoidable accident such as death befell it.
the man and the woman are the same regarding the law of bailees. Their law is equal.

my teachers ruled that he does not swear on the claim of a minor etc.. Although one does not swear on the claim of a minor since his claim is not considered a claim, if a minor made a deposit and the deposit was lost, the bailee must swear to him, since the bailee's oath does not arise from a certain claim of the depositor, and a minor is no different in it from an adult (see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 5:9).

just as they instituted drawing for purchasers. By Torah law movable property can be acquired by giving money, and the Sages instituted that it is not acquired by money but only by lifting or drawing (see Hilchot Mekhirah 3:1).

so they instituted drawing for bailees. The Sages instituted that bailment takes effect only after drawing, both regarding the obligation of guarding and the bailee's responsibility, and regarding the depositor or lender not being able to retract (Maggid Mishneh).

and he said to him, 'put it down before you,' he is an unpaid bailee. Although they instituted that bailment takes effect only through drawing, some explained that there was indeed drawing, but in cases where he said 'put it before you' and the like, even if there was drawing, no obligation of guarding applies to him; and some explained that this speaks of the bailee's courtyard, which acquires for him without drawing (see Meiri, Bava Metzia 80b and other Rishonim there).
he is neither an unpaid bailee nor a paid bailee. For these statements contain no language of commitment but are like saying 'put your item before you and guard it yourself' and the like.

but he imposes a ban etc.. By an enactment of the Geonim, in certain cases when a person suspects another and cannot obligate him to take an oath, he can impose a ban (a curse) in general on whoever lies against him in that matter, without mentioning the name of the suspect (see Hilchot Gezelah 4:7-8, Maggid Mishneh, Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:4).

for we do not say 'migo' to exempt him from an oath but to exempt him from paying. A 'migo' claim is when a defendant could make a better claim that would exempt him from the monetary claim, and makes a lesser claim. The law is that he is exempt from the monetary claim even with the lesser claim, because he could have made the better claim ('migo' is an Aramaic word meaning 'since'; for an example of a migo claim see Hilchot Zekhiyah u-Matanah 9:22-23). The rule is that a migo claim is effective to exempt the defendant from monetary liability, but does not exempt him from an oath he is obligated to take (for further examples see Hilchot Sheluchin ve-Shutafin 9:4, Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 13:3). Therefore in a case where the deposit was made with him without witnesses, although he could have made a better claim, denying that he is a bailee and being exempt, and instead made a lesser claim, admitting he is a bailee but that the deposit was lost by accident, stolen or lost, he is not exempt from an oath.

even if the item... was worth a perutah, the bailee swears about it. The law here is not like the oath of one who admits part of a claim, who is obligated to swear only for denying the value of two silver ma'ah or more (see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 3:1). However, if the deposit is worth less than a perutah, one does not swear the deposit oath about it unless it is a vessel (see ibid. 3:5-6, Hilchot Shevu'ot 7:16).

and none of the bailees needs a partial admission. The obligation of an oath for bailees applies even when he claims the entire deposit was lost by accident, stolen or lost, unlike the law of one who partially admits, who is obligated to swear only if he admitted part and denied part (Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 3:1).
an unpaid bailee may stipulate etc.. One may stipulate in advance a change in the bailee's liability, both to make it lighter and to make it stricter.
and no kinyan or witnesses are needed. No kinyan sudar or witnesses are needed to give the stipulation force.
this one claimed that there was a stipulation. The depositor claims there was a stipulation in his favor, for example that the bailee undertook to be liable even in cases where he should be exempt.

the bailee swears the bailees' oath and includes in it that there was no stipulation. The bailee must swear about what happened to the deposit like any bailee, and includes in his oath ('rolls into it') also an oath that there was no stipulation between them (for the principle of rolling an oath see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:12; and so too in the opposite case, where the bailee claims there was a stipulation, he rolls into his oath that there was one - Hilchot She'elah u-Pikadon 6:2).
'put it down before you,' and I did not become a bailee for him. By this statement he does not become a bailee (as above, halakhah 8).

he swears a heset oath. For the bailees' oath obligation applies only when he admits that he is a bailee, but when he denies it, he is like one who denies everything, who is not obligated by Torah law to take an oath while holding an object, but rather a heset oath, a lighter oath by rabbinic law without holding an object.
for he accepted it only in this manner. By saying 'put it before you'.
and he includes in his oath. By way of rolling an oath.

that he did not lay a hand on it, nor destroy it by hand, nor cause it to be lost in a way that makes him liable to pay. For if he laid a hand on it he is considered a robber and is liable even for accidents (Hilchot Gezelah 3:11), and if he destroyed it by hand or caused it damage for which one is liable for causing, he is liable as a damager (see Hilchot Chovel u-Mazik 7:7).
when does this apply. That for one who claims 'I returned it to you,' a heset oath suffices.
a document. Attesting to his commitment to guard.
he swears while holding an object. He swears while holding a Torah scroll, similar to one who takes a Torah oath (see Hilchot Shevu'ot 11:8).

because since he could say etc.. The reason they do not obligate him to pay even though the depositor has a document is that he has a 'migo' claim: since he could have claimed that the deposit was stolen or lost, he is believed on his claim that he returned it.

and just as if he claimed it was lost by accident, he swears by Torah law while holding an object etc.. Because the 'migo' is based on a claim that would have required him to take the bailees' oath by Torah law while holding an object, the Sages instituted that he swear a severe oath while holding an object, resembling an oath of the Torah.
when the bailee could claim that they were lost by accident and we would not require him to bring proof. In which case the migo claim exists.

but if he was obligated to bring proof of his claim, as will be explained. For example where the accident occurred in a place where many people are present, and he must bring witnesses and may not swear (below 3:1).
he is not believed to say 'I returned it'. Because he has no migo claim in this case, since in any event he would have had to bring witnesses.
but only this bailee against whom there is a document. Because the migo in this case is based on a claim that involves an oath while holding an object, as above.
a bailee who claimed that a major accident befell it, such as it was broken and died. Both an unpaid bailee and a paid bailee are exempt by an oath for this accident.
and if he does not bring proof, he must pay. And he is not exempt by an oath.
who carried a jug of wine for hire. His law is that of a paid bailee.
Mechoza. A city in Babylonia.
rather, you stumbled and fell. And the Sages instituted that one who stumbles is considered subject to accident, and even a paid bailee is exempt from paying (as below, 5:2).

for this is not a major accident, and breakage is like theft and loss, for which he is liable. When he stumbled and the jug broke, this is not considered a major accident, for he should have walked more carefully, but its law is like theft and loss, for which a paid bailee must pay by Torah law.
but the Sages instituted that he be liable to swear that he was not negligent with it. Like the law of a paid bailee for a major accident.

it is like an accident and is not an accident. On one hand this load is not heavy for two people, and so they did not load themselves beyond measure; on the other, it may be that precisely because there were two, each relied on the other and loosened his grip to lighten his load, and they should have divided the load from the start so that each would carry half alone (see the next passage).
and they pay half if there are witnesses that they were not negligent with it. For where witnesses are available, they cannot swear.
they swear that they did not break it through negligence. And thereby they are exempt from the half that was judged as accident.
if he returned it on market day etc.. That the payment is assessed according to the value of a jug of wine on the day of payment.
and this is when he had no wine to sell on market day. For if the jug had existed, he would have sold it now, and so he lost four.
but if he had wine, they return three to him. Because he can sell other jugs that he has, he lost only three.
they return three to him. The value of the jug on an ordinary day that is not market day.

and they deduct from him at all times etc.. Whether on market day or not, they deduct from the payment the effort of selling the wine in the jug had it existed, and the hole he would have made in it to take out wine for buyers, which reduces the value of the jug (Sma, 304:11).
if it was a single wolf, this is not an accident. Since the shepherd can drive it off, this is not considered a major accident from which a paid bailee is exempt, and he must pay.
even at the time of the wolf attacks. When wolves come out of their hiding places to waylay passersby everywhere.
and if there were two wolves, it is an accident. For he has no power to drive them off, and it is classed as an accident in which even a paid bailee is exempt.
an armed robber. An armed bandit.

and the burdeles. It seems that the reference here is to a hyena (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Kamma 1:4, Aruch ha-Shalem, entry 'burdeles' and 'appa'). [Note: Maimonides in the Commentary on the Mishnah vocalizes the word differently.]
these are accidents. And even a paid bailee is exempt from paying.
when they came on their own. When wild animals or robbers came to the animals' usual grazing place.
to a place where packs of beasts and robbers gather. A place where they band together and assemble.
these are not accidents and he must pay. For his actions caused it and he is considered negligent.
to save the animal torn or taken captive, with other shepherds and with sticks. To rescue an animal from being torn or captured by calling other shepherds to help him or by bringing weapons.
both a paid bailee and an unpaid bailee. Both are required to call shepherds and bring sticks.
he calls shepherds and brings sticks without payment. He is required to bring the help of other shepherds or weapons without payment.

up to the value of the animal in order to save it. Even if the cost of the rescue reaches the value of the animal, it is better for the owner to spare himself the trouble of buying new animals, or the trouble of training the new animals he would buy (Bava Metzia 93b).

for he can claim only up to their value, and he could have said it was torn. The maximum sum he can claim to have spent on the rescue is the value of the animal, and he is believed to collect this sum from the owners, since he could have claimed that it was torn and taken it for himself.
like the law of all who swear and collect. See Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:2.
whether at a time when shepherds customarily go in. When the animals graze in a quiet and safe place, the shepherds go into the city for their affairs.

or at a time when shepherds do not customarily go in etc.. Although his entering the city is negligence, and one who is negligent at the start and subject to accident at the end is liable (as above 1:4), since the accident is not a direct result of the negligence - for even had he been there he could not have saved it - he is exempt (see also below, halakhah 10).
we do not say, 'had he been there he would have saved it'. And since he was not, he would have to pay.
he afflicted it and it died. He tormented the animal by hunger or by work and lack of proper care and the like, and it died as a result.
it is not an accident. And it is even classed as negligence, and both a paid bailee and an unpaid bailee are liable for it (Maggid Mishneh).

it overpowered him and went up to the tops of cliffs, and it overpowered him and fell. Although he held onto the animal, it overpowered him and went up to the tops of the cliffs, and although he tried to keep it from falling, it overpowered him and fell.
even though it overpowered him and fell and died or was broken. Although he tried to keep it from falling.
to the river's current. The flood of a river where the flow is strong.
he is liable... for the bailee takes payment only to guard with excellent guarding. But an unpaid bailee is exempt in this case.
was negligent with it. Did not guard it properly.

for its going out did not cause it to come to this accident. A bailee who is negligent at the start and subject to accident at the end is not liable unless there is a connection between the negligence and the accident.
even though he is an unpaid bailee. For an unpaid bailee is liable for negligence.

for even if it did not die, it is lost in the thief's hand, and its going out caused it to be stolen. For at the time the animal was stolen he was already liable because he was negligent, and its later natural death does not exempt him.
it slipped. And was broken or died.

he is exempt even though he went against the owners' wishes. For the danger of slipping exists more on a mountain than in a valley, so it turns out that the death was not caused by his changing from the owners' wishes.
and if it was overheated, he is liable. For the danger of overheating exists more in a valley than on a mountain, so it turns out that the death was caused by his changing from the owners' wishes.
the ascent. The slope of the mountain.

and likewise one who rents the cow. And also rented with it the plowshare, which is a plowing tool with a curved head that digs the ground. Their custom was that together with the cow two workers were also hired for the plowing, one holding the plowshare to direct it and the other goading the animal (see Bava Metzia 80a and the Rishonim there).
the renter is exempt. For the valley soil is easier to plow than mountain soil, so the breaking of the plowshare was not caused by his changing from the owners' wishes.

and the law of the owner of the cow with the craftsmen who plowed. The workers are liable for breaking the plowshare because they should have been careful while plowing, and they must pay the lessor as will be explained shortly.
the renter is liable. For the damage was caused by his changing from the owners' wishes.
and the law of the renter with the craftsmen. The renter can claim from the workers because they had to be careful in any case.

the one who holds the tool during plowing. The worker who directs the plowshare is liable to pay, because he did not direct the plowshare properly and so it broke, and the worker who goads the animal is exempt.
in terraces. A terraced field that is not uniform.
both are liable for the price of the plowshare. In a terraced place both must be careful to prevent the tool from breaking, and therefore both are liable.
with a goad. A stick used to drive the animal.
to thresh legumes. Threshing is separating the kernels from the stalk, done by driving the animal over the grain.
and he threshed grain and it slipped, he is exempt. For in threshing grain the danger of slipping is less than in threshing legumes.
it makes slippery. It makes things slick.

since there are witnesses testifying that the water in the Pekod River is available. That everyone knows there is water in this river, and it is considered as though witnesses testify to it (Rashi, Bava Metzia 81b); or it means that witnesses did testify that there is water in the Pekod River (so Rabbeinu Chananel appears to have explained, cited in Shitah Mekubetzet there; and see also Rabbeinu Yehonatan cited there).

and we do not say, 'why would I lie where there are witnesses'. Although he has a migo claim, since he could have claimed that he went by a different route, a migo claim is not effective where witnesses testify against his present claim.
ritlin. A unit of weight.

because bulk is hard on the load, and barley has bulk. The specific gravity of barley is less than that of wheat, and one who brings a load of barley equal in weight to a load of wheat increases the load's volume, so the animal's death was caused by the renter's changing from the owners' wishes.
by its weight. By the same weight.
straw. And the volume of straw is greater than the volume of grain.
but if he rented it to bring barley on it and brought wheat of the same weight. And thereby reduced the volume of the load on the animal.
he may not have a woman ride on it. Because carrying a woman is more burdensome than carrying a man (Sefer ha-Ner, Bava Metzia 89b; and see a similar explanation in Chasdei David, Bava Metzia 7:6).
even a pregnant woman who is nursing. For the fetus in her womb adds to the load, and she also holds in her arms the baby she is nursing.
defined. Specified.
a thirtieth part. One thirtieth of the weight agreed on with the lessor.
but he pays the rent for the excess. For the rent is for loading a certain weight, and he must pay the additional rent for the additional weight he loaded.
he rented it without specification. Without their having fixed between them the weight the animal would carry.
the porter. A laborer who carries loads on his shoulder.
who added a kav to his load. The person who hired him added a kav to his load without his knowledge.

for even though he is a person of understanding and feels the weight of the load. And this was a reason to exempt the hirer who loaded excess weight on him, on the claim that the porter accepted the additional weight on himself.

it may occur to him that this heaviness is because of his illness. The porter may think that the load is heavier on him than usual because of his weakness, and therefore the hirer should not be exempt on that account.
he is permitted. He is allowed.
and his flask. A jug of water for drinking.
and his provisions for that journey. Food enough for him until he reaches his final destination.
to search. To look for.
lodging. A place to stay overnight.
more than this. If he wants to load the donkey with more than this.
to the donkey driver. The one who leads the donkey on the road for the hirer (the 'chamar').
barley, straw and provisions for that day. Barley and straw for the donkey, and food for himself for that day only.
because he can buy at each and every lodging. That is the donkey driver's way (but the hirer does not do this, and so he may put on it provisions for the entire journey - Bava Metzia 79b).

or was taken for the king's service even though it will not return. The authorities seized the donkey for the king's service and will not return it (all the more so if the donkey was taken only for a time and will be returned afterward).

if it was taken in the course of its going. When the authorities' agents were not looking for this particular animal but came upon it by chance, the renter must pay, because the lessor can argue that the renter's luck caused it, as had he not led the animal there it would not have been taken; but if they took this animal specifically, it is on account of the lessor and not the renter, and he must provide another animal (Tosafot, Bava Metzia 78b, citing Rabbeinu Chananel).
and he must give him his rent in full. The renter must pay the entire rent.

but if he rented it to ride or to carry glass vessels and the like, he must provide him a donkey. When he rented the animal for riding or for carrying a fragile load, the lessor has a stronger obligation to fulfil the rental (Yad Peshutah).
and if he did not provide one, he returns the rent. If the renter already paid the rent, the lessor returns it to him.
and he calculates with him for the rent of what he traveled on it. The renter pays the lessor proportionally for the part of the rental that was fulfilled.

if he said to him 'a donkey' without specification... he must provide him another donkey in any case. And he cannot say 'what is yours is before you,' since he undertook to rent him a donkey and there is no donkey here, because it died or became unusable (unlike the previous halakhah, where the animal exists but the renter can no longer use it).

the renter may sell the animal and buy another animal with the proceeds. He may sell the animal that died or was broken and buy with its price another animal to use for the rental, and afterward it returns to the owners.

or hire with the proceeds if the proceeds are not enough to buy, until he reaches the place agreed with him. If the sale proceeds do not suffice to buy another animal, he may hire another animal with them to fulfil the rental as agreed between them.
he said to him, 'this donkey I am renting'. If they did not agree in general on renting a donkey but agreed on renting a specific donkey.

if he rented it to ride or for glass vessels. When he rented the animal for riding or for carrying a fragile load, the lessor has a stronger obligation to fulfil the rental, and therefore even if the specific donkey they agreed on died, the lessor's obligation to the renter did not lapse.
and he has against him only a complaint. The renter may be displeased with the lessor, but cannot claim money from him.
and he leaves its carcass to him. To the lessor, and he cannot hire another donkey with the proceeds of the carcass.
this ship... wine without specification. That at the time of the rental they agreed on a particular ship in which the renter would carry whatever wine he wished, and not a particular wine.

even though he gave him the rent, he returns all the rent, for this one says to him etc.. Because the lessor cannot fulfil his commitment to supply this specific ship, whereas the renter can fulfil his part by bringing other wine, the lessor must return the full rent to the renter (and unlike the law of the animal mentioned in the previous halakhah, here the renter need not pay the lessor the rent for half the journey, because the wine sank and he did not benefit from the rental at all).

for there is great concern about the ship. For even if the lessor wanted to provide the renter another ship, the renter can claim that he rented this ship specifically because it was suited to carrying the wine.

a ship without specification... this wine. That at the time of the rental they agreed that the renter would carry a particular wine, without commitment to a particular ship that the lessor would supply to the renter.

he must pay all the rent, for the lessor says to him etc.. Because the renter cannot fulfil his part of the commitment, whereas the lessor can fulfil his part by supplying another ship, the renter must pay the rent.

but he must deduct for him the effort of half the journey. The lessor of the ship deducts from the rent the effort of half the journey that he was supposed to sail the ship had it not sunk, and one calculates how much a person would be willing to have deducted from his wage for the effort of sailing that distance in exchange for sitting idle instead of sailing.

for this one cannot bring the ship itself and that one cannot bring the wine itself. And since neither can fulfil his part of the rental agreement, the money is left in the hand of the one who holds it.

he rented a ship without specification for wine without specification, they divide the rent. Since each can fulfil his part of the rental agreement, but neither is interested in carrying out the rental, they divide the rent between them.
and unloaded it in the middle of the journey. The renter unloaded his cargo from it in the middle of the journey.
he pays him the rent for the whole journey. The renter pays the lessor the full rent, although he did not use all of it.

whoever will rent it to him up to the place agreed. If the renter finds another person to rent the ship from him and use it subject to what was agreed with the first lessor, he may do so (as below 5:5).
and the ship's owner has a complaint against him. For he rented to another without his knowledge, and perhaps the lessor is not comfortable renting to this person.
and he got off and the buyer got on. The renter who sold his merchandise gets off the ship, and the buyer gets on and continues the voyage.
but to others who are like the number of his household. The renter's permission to substitute tenants is conditional on his not increasing the number of occupants.
for the Sages said that a renter may not sublet etc.. As above 1:4.
for he says to him. The lessor can argue against the renter.
but with land. That wherever it is, it does not leave the owner's domain (Meiri, Bava Metzia 79b).
or a ship, since its owner is with it. For the ship's owner sails with the renter.
he is not obligated to build it. Since he rented him a specific house, the lessor is not obligated to build the house, and the rental ended when it fell.

rather he calculates with him for what he used and returns to him the rest of the rent. In this case the renter does not use the value of the fallen house to build or rent another, because one does not sell a fallen house (unlike the one who rents this donkey for riding, where the renter uses the value of the carcass to buy or rent another donkey as above 5:2, since a carcass is something that stands to be sold - Maggid Mishneh).
if he demolished it. If the lessor tore down the house.
he must provide him another house or rent him one like it. For when this results from a direct act of the lessor, he must provide the renter another house to rent.
a violent man. A violent person who takes by force.
who cancelled the first rental. He nullified the rental against the renter's will.

he rented him a house without specification etc.. Since at the time of the rental they did not agree on a particular house, the lessor must fulfil his part of the rental and provide the renter a house.
that it be called a house. That it be a house fit for dwelling.
such a house. They defined the house to be rented by reference to another house.
and he cannot say to him, 'my words did not concern etc.'. The lessor cannot claim that by the word 'such' he meant other aspects of this house that he showed him.
therefore. If the house fell and the lessor came to rebuild it.
he may not make it into two. Divided into two.

one who rents an upper room without specification must provide him an upper room. If the upper floor (the 'aliyah') fell, the lessor must provide the renter an upper room fit for dwelling (and if he said 'this upper room' or 'an upper room like this' and it fell, the law is the same as stated above regarding a house).
the upper room was breached by four handbreadths. The floor of the upper room broke or loosened and dropped down over an area of four handbreadths by four handbreadths.
and if he did not repair it, the renter etc.. Because when the lessor said 'this upper room above this house,' he pledged the house for the integrity of the upper room.
if there were two upper rooms one above the other and the upper one was breached. A three-story building and the third floor, where the renter lived, was breached.
the lower one was breached. The lower upper room, which is the second floor of the building, was breached.

it is doubtful whether he lives in the upper one or in the house. On one hand the lessor can argue that he undertook to rent him an upper room, and he fulfils his part of the agreement when the renter lives on the third floor; on the other, the renter can argue that he did not accept upon himself the trouble of climbing to the third floor and that he wants to live on the first floor, in the lessor's house (Bava Metzia 117a).
therefore he may not live. He may not live in the house, on the first floor. Because of the doubt, he cannot take the full right of dwelling in the house from the owner, who is in possession of it.
and if he lives there, he is not removed. If the renter got there first and took hold of his right to live in the house, he is not removed from it, since he is now in possession of the house.
this vine that is trained over this peach tree. This vine that is trained on this peach tree.
you must keep the peach tree standing as long as the vine exists. Because by his statement he pledged the peach tree to the vine.

one who rents a house to his fellow in a large birah. He rented him a dwelling unit inside a birah, which is a large rectangular structure containing small dwelling units. In the center of the birah there is a kind of open space for the entry of light and air, and in this space an ornamental garden (tarbetz) is planted, and behind the houses around the perimeter of the birah there is a large courtyard surrounded by walls separating it from the public domain (Meiri, Bava Batra 6a).
its protrusions. Projections coming out of the walls on which things can be hung.
and its walls. For example to place objects in a niche of the wall or to drive nails into it and hang objects on it.

up to four cubits. Along the wall up to a distance of four cubits from the opening of his house, even though it is opposite the area of another house (Rashi and Tosafot R. Yehuda he-Chasid there). Some explain that along this length he may use it up to a height of four cubits (Yad Ramah and Meiri there).
and in the tarbetz. In the walls and air of the small garden in the space between the houses.

in the thickness of the walls. By hanging projections or carving small windows for placing objects (Meiri there); some explain that this speaks of an upper dwelling that uses the area of the wall's thickness from above (Rashi, Tosafot R. Yehuda he-Chasid and Yad Ramah there).
in the way we said regarding purchase and sale. See Hilchot Mekhirah 26:7-8.
without specification. Without detail.
to set up doors for him. To install doors in the doorways.
and to open windows for him that have become spoiled. Openings made in walls that serve as windows and that tend to become blocked with time.
and to support the beam that broke. To provide support for the roof beam if it broke and there is concern that it will collapse.
a bolt. A bar, a rod placed across the door from end to end that serves to lock the house from the inside.
and a lock. Which serves to lock the house from the outside.
the work of a craftsman. And not just anyone can make them.
a major fundamental. A basic item.

the renter must make a parapet. For there is a commandment to make a parapet on the roof of a house so that people do not fall from it (Hilchot Rotze'ach 11:1), and this commandment falls on the one who lives in the house.
and a mezuzah. For affixing the mezuzah is the obligation of the one who lives in the house (see Hilchot Mezuzah 5:11).
the place of the mezuzah. The place for putting up the mezuzah.
to plaster its roof. To coat the roof with clay to seal it against rain penetration.
and it was breached by four. The floor of the upper room was damaged over an area of four handbreadths by four handbreadths (see above 5:8).
the ceiling and the plaster layer above it. The beams from which the ceiling is built and the clay covering over the beams.
the dung. Animal droppings.

it belongs to the renter, therefore he is responsible for taking it out. Since the dung belongs to the renter if he wishes to use it, the duty to remove it, if he does not want to use it, falls on him.
and if the animals belonged to others. That animals that belong neither to the renter nor to the lessor entered the courtyard and dropped dung there.

for a person's courtyard acquires for him without his knowledge. His courtyard is like an agent acquiring on his behalf, and he acquired this dung (see also Hilchot Gezelah va-Avedah 17:8-10, Hilchot Zekhiyah u-Matanah 4:8-9).

a house without specification for lodging is no less than one day. When the rental was agreed for lodging and it was not agreed for how many days, the rental is for the night and the following day and not for the night alone (Shitah Mekubetzet, Bava Metzia 101b).

for Shabbat rest, no less than two days. When the rental was agreed with the wording 'shevitah,' since in order to rest on Shabbat a person needs to prepare his resting place on Friday and rest on Shabbat, this wording includes a day, a night and a day up to the following night (ibid.; and see Chasdei David, Bava Metzia 8:11, who explained the Shitah Mekubetzet differently and brought another explanation of his own).
for marriage, no less than thirty days. For the celebration of marriage lasts thirty days (see Hilchot Berakhot 5:5).
without specification. And they did not fix a time for the rental.
in order to seek a place. To look for other housing.

but in the rainy season he may not remove him from the festival until Passover. Since in the rainy season it is hard for a person to move himself from house to house and rental homes are not available, he cannot remove him from the festival of Sukkot until Passover even if he gives notice thirty days beforehand.
if any of the thirty days remain, even one day, after the festival etc.. If the thirty days were not completed before the festival, but one day remains after the festival begins.

and only if he notifies him thirty days beforehand. Even at the end of Passover he cannot remove him immediately on the basis of the notice given before the rainy season, and must notify him again thirty days before the end of Passover.
in towns. In villages.
but in large cities. In large cities, since many want to live in them, housing is not available there, and therefore the period of advance notice to the tenant is longer.

and likewise with a shop he must notify him twelve months in advance. Because a shopkeeper customarily gives his customers credit, buyers must be given time to pay their debts in order to prevent loss to the shopkeeper; or because the effort of finding a replacement shop and moving to it is greater than finding and moving to a dwelling (see Meiri, Bava Metzia 101b).
so the renter must notify him. If he wishes to end the rental.

so that he can look for a tenant and his house not remain vacant. That the lessor look for a new tenant for the house that became vacant; in large cities this requires more time, since people customarily rent for a long period and tenants are not always found (Aruch HaShulchan 312:17).
he cannot leave, but must pay the rent. He cannot leave before the time is up unless he pays the rent through the end of thirty days in towns or the end of twelve months in large cities.
the lessor may. He has permission.

or rent at the full price until you find or leave. He stipulates with him that he will pay rent at the higher price until he finds another dwelling or leaves immediately. In this case the lessor is not obligated to give him time to leave, because he is losing money.
rent for me. Rent to me.
the lessor's house in which he lived fell. And it turns out the lessor has nowhere to live.
he may remove the renter from his house. Immediately, and need not give him time to find a dwelling.
he gave the house to his son to marry a woman in it. After he rented it to another, his son found a wife and he wanted to give him the house and remove the renter.
the second. The buyer, recipient of the gift, or heir.
until he notifies him etc.. In the case where he rented without specification (and if he rented for a defined period, he cannot remove him until the end of the rental period).

just as a person may stipulate any condition he wishes in purchase and sale etc.. Whether the seller stipulated or the buyer stipulated, the condition stands (see Hilchot Mekhirah 11:1), and so too with rental.
for a rental is a sale for a fixed time. A rental is a type of sale limited in time.

and anyone whose sale of his property is a valid sale etc.. To exclude the imbecile, whose sale has no validity, and also the deaf-mute and the minor, whose ability to sell is limited (see ibid., chapter 29).
and whoever cannot sell cannot rent. Things that cannot be sold cannot be rented either (such as something not yet in the world and other things; see ibid., chapters 22-23).

unless he has only the produce of that land, in which case he rents and does not sell. One who has the right to eat the produce and has no right in the land itself may rent the right to eat the produce to another, even though he cannot sell the land itself (and he can also sell the right to eat the produce - Responsa Maharik 20).
one who rents a house to his fellow for a year. If they agreed in advance on a certain sum for a full year.
and the year was intercalated, it is intercalated for the renter. If the court decided to intercalate the year and add a month to it, the renter need not add to the rent for the added month.
he rented by the month, the intercalation is for the lessor. If they agreed on monthly rent, the renter must pay rent for the additional month.

for the land is presumed to belong to its owner. Since we are uncertain about these expressions, whether the main thing is the yearly sum or the monthly sum, the law favors the owner of the land, who is in possession of it even though it is not in his hand now (see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 11:1; and see a similar case in Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 27:16 regarding doubt in the wording of ketubah documents).
I rented to you for this time. And according to his claim he can remove him at the end of that time without advance notice (as above 6:6).
but without specification. Without limit, in which case the lessor cannot evict him without advance notice (ibid., halakhah 7).
or for a long time. A defined time, but longer than the lessor claims.
the homeowner swears a heset oath. An oath that the Sages instituted for one who denies the entire claim against him (Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:3).
and removes him from the house. Because land is presumed to belong to its owner.

whether the rental was by document or by witnesses. Whether there is a rental contract or there were witnesses to the rental agreement made orally, this has no bearing on the renter's credibility in claiming that he paid.
if he claimed him within thirty days. And in a rental without specification, the renter must pay the lessor every thirty days (Mirkevet ha-Mishneh).

the renter must bring proof. Because the obligation to pay for each period of time arises only at its end, and the assumption is that a person does not pay his debt before its due date (see Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 11:6).
or he pays and imposes a ban. If the renter has no proof, he must pay, and before paying he may impose a ban (a curse - see above 2:8 for explanation) on whoever holds his money improperly.

or he may claim against him for the money he gave first. Another option is that after paying he sues the lessor for having paid him twice and demands back the first payment, and the lessor must swear a heset oath that he did not receive it, since he denies the entire claim.
and even on the thirtieth day. Which is the last day of the rental, he is believed when claiming that he paid, since a person may pay on the last day of the rental.
the lessor must bring proof. Since it is possible that he paid him, and the claimant must bring proof of his words.
even on the twenty-ninth of Elul. Like the law of a renter for thirty days who claimed he paid on the thirtieth day, who is believed.
and it has no date. The document has no date indicating when the rental began.
the renter must bring proof. Because the land is presumed to belong to the owner (as above, halakhah 2).
or if he held a pledge. And he eats its produce as part of the repayment of the debt (see Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 6:7).
and land is purchased with them. That will belong to the lessor.
and he eats its produce. The lessee or the lender receives the produce of the land.

and the body of the trees... both of them are forbidden because of the interest of the lender and the borrower. One cannot give the lender the value of the trees as payment of the full principal of the loan, because then it turns out that the produce he already ate was given as interest; likewise one cannot give the trees to the borrower so that he repays the full amount of the loan from his own funds, because then the produce the lender already ate would be interest (Maggid Mishneh; and see Even ha-Azel and Mirkevet ha-Mishneh, who explained the prohibition of interest in this case in different ways; and see Lechem Mishneh, that this prohibition applies only to a pledge and not to a lease).
the owner of the produce. The lessee or the pledgee, who eat the produce.
and this lessee or lender got ahead and ate the produce. Of the third year.

the produce is presumed to belong to those who ate it, until the owner of the land brings proof. Although generally the lessee must bring proof, since land is presumed to remain in its owner's possession, in this case, since the matter will be revealed when the witnesses signed on the document come and testify to its meaning, we do not trouble the court to convene twice (both now and when the witnesses come); rather, we leave the produce in the hands of the one who ate it until the matter is clarified (Bavli Bava Metzia 110a).
the pledgee. The one with whom the field is pledged.

and he withheld the document and said, "I have produce for five years". He claimed that he has two more years of eating the produce of the land, and the document is not before us to clarify the matter.
they said to him, "Bring your document". They told the lessee or pledgee to show the document in his possession, so that it can be seen for how many years it is leased or pledged to him.

for if he wished he could have said, "It is purchased and in my hands," since he has eaten it for three years. After three years of using a field without protest from the owner, the possessor is believed when he claims that he bought it (see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 11:2). And since he could have claimed that the field is his, he is believed to claim that the lease period is longer than the owners claim (and if the owners wanted to prevent him from making this claim, they would have had to protest within the three years - Bavli Bava Metzia 110a).
or he misled him until he brought in his produce. He deceived his fellow and caused him to bring his produce into his house.

that he must inform the court. That he must inform the court before he removes the produce from his house (Sma, 359:2), and some explain that he informs the court after he has taken the produce out to the market (Beit Yosef).
and they rent a place with part of their proceeds. They use part of the proceeds of the produce to rent a place in which to store the produce for the owners.
because of the duty to return a lost item to its owners. Since this prevents them from suffering a loss.
even though he acted improperly. The owner of the produce.
One who rents a mill from his fellow etc.. They agreed between them that the rent would not be paid in money, but that the lessee would grind a certain quantity of wheat each month for the lessor.
and the mill owner became wealthy and no longer needs to grind there. He acquired a mill for himself and does not need the lessee's grinding, and wants the rent to be paid in money.
if the lessee has wheat that he needs to grind, for himself or for others. If the work of the mill grinding the lessee's wheat or others' wheat is enough for the lessee, he pays the lessor in money.
for this is the way of Sodom. Preventing another from benefiting when he himself suffers no loss thereby (see Hilchot Shekhenim 7:8).
Whether one rents from his fellow... for money. That he pays fixed rent for the field or vineyard, and the produce is his.
or he rented from him for a fixed quantity of produce. That the rent is paid in a set quantity of crop, regardless of what the field yielded.
a kor. A measure of volume of thirty se'ah.
and to spend expenses on it. To fund from his own pocket the costs of working the field.
for the fence of the land. For the main fencing and guarding of the field.
on the owner of the land. Since work tools are an essential need, supplying them is the responsibility of the field's owner.
and digging the places in which water is collected. Channels for collecting water for irrigation.
on the lessee or on the sharecropper. Since they are not essential and are meant to ease the work of irrigation.
for a few years. Fewer than seven years.
he may not sow it with flax. Because its roots remain in the soil for a long time, which weakens the soil and harms its cultivation for six years (Maggid Mishneh).
if he rented it or took it as a sharecropper for seven years, he sows it with flax in the first year. So that in this way the soil will return to its previous condition at the end of the period.

and the seventh year is not counted etc.. When they agreed on seven years, they meant seven years of cultivation, so the Shemittah year, in which the field cannot be worked, is not included in the agreement; whereas when they agreed on a "shavua" (a week), meaning a cycle of seven years, the Shemittah year is included in the agreement.
a beit ha-shelahin. A field of crops that needs much irrigation.
a beit ha-ilan. An orchard of trees.
and the spring of the beit ha-shelahin dried up. The water source of this field was damaged.
or the tree was cut down. And the yield of the orchard decreased.
he does not deduct from his lease payment. He does not reduce what was agreed that he would give him for leasing the field.
a blow affecting the whole region. A disaster that struck the entire area and not only this particular field, and cannot be attributed to the actions or luck of the lessee or sharecropper.

he deducts from his lease payment. In a lease or tenancy arrangement he pays the field's owner less than what was agreed, and in sharecropping the field's owner receives a smaller share than originally agreed (see Mirkevet ha-Mishneh).
he was standing in the field. When they agreed on the lease.

and he did not say "this" except as one who says, "as it is now I lease to you". So it turns out that the added word "this" is like a condition, that he leases it to him on the understanding that it has a spring or a tree.
was blighted. The crop that the field produced dried up.
if this happened to most of the fields of that city. So it turns out that this is a blow affecting the whole region.
everything according to the loss that befell him. The deduction is proportional to the loss caused to the crop.

he does not deduct from his lease payment even though all the fields of the landowner were blighted. Even if all of the landowner's fields were damaged, the lessee or sharecropper cannot attribute the loss to the landowner and claim that it was caused by Heaven because of him.
most of the fields. Of the city.

for the loss depends only on the lessee, since all his fields were blighted. When all the lessee's fields were blighted, we attribute to him the loss of the leased field as well (for the reason for the distinction between this case and the previous one, see Bavli Bava Metzia 106a).

he does not deduct from his lease payment. For the owner of the field can claim that had he sown as agreed, perhaps the crop would not have been damaged; and likewise, if he sowed and it did not grow, the owner can claim that he should have sown again.
and until when is he obligated to see to it and sow another time if it did not sprout. And if he did not do so, he deducts from his lease payment.

as long as it is fit for sowing in that place. And if the lessee or sharecropper sowed again during this time and the grain did not grow, the field's owner deducts from the rent or the sharecropping share.
a place where it is customary to reap. To cut the grain with a sickle or scythe and leave the stalks attached to the ground.
and he may not uproot. To pull up the grain from the root.

and each can hold the other back. For the field's owner can claim that he wants reaping so that the stalks remain in the ground for fertilizing, or that he wants uprooting so that his land is cleared; and the lessee or sharecropper can claim that he wants reaping because it is easier, or that he wants uprooting so as to use the straw to feed his animals (Bavli Bava Metzia 103b).
and a place where it is customary to plow after it. To plow after the uprooting or reaping in order to turn over the soil and prepare it for the next sowing.

a place where it is customary to lease trees together with the land etc.. In a place where it is customary that one who leases land eats the fruit incidentally to the lease, even though he does not work the trees, the lessee acquires it even if they did not stipulate this explicitly. And even if the rent is lower than usual, we do not say that the field's owner lowered the rent on the understanding that he himself would take the fruit of the trees. And likewise the reverse.
if it was blighted he gives him from it. Even if the crop that grew is flawed, he may give him from it what he undertook to give.
for ten baskets of grapes. In return for ten baskets full of grapes.
that turned sour. That became sour.
but if he leased it for ten jars of wine and it turned sour, he must give him good wine. For the vineyard's crop was not blighted; rather, the wine made from it turned sour.
alfalfa. Alfalfa, fodder.

or he first sowed it with alfalfa, plowed it, and afterward sowed it again and it was blighted. And the lessee wants to give him of the alfalfa he sowed the second time (and this speaks of a case where the lessee took it on the understanding that he would sow alfalfa once, and when he sowed it twice he deviated - Lechem Mishneh).
for he deviated. And with any deviation the field's owner can claim that he did not intend to accept the crop that grew after the deviation.
to weed. To clear the soil of weeds.
"I am giving you your lease payment". The same quantity of grain that I undertook.
"tomorrow you will leave it, and it will bring up weeds before me". For the bad weeds that the lessee leaves in the field will ruin the future growth of grain.
"in the end I will plow it". After I reap the grain I will plow it in order to uproot the weeds.
we do not listen to him. Because in the meantime seeds from the weeds will fall and remain after the plowing and will sprout, so they must be weeded in advance.

because wheat weakens the soil more than barley. And the lessee may not sow a species that harms the soil more than the species agreed upon, but he may sow a species that harms it less. This is determined by those who work in plowing and cultivating land in that place and who know the nature of the soil and the seeds sown in it (Perush ha-Mishnayot, Bava Metzia 9:8).
legumes. Legumes.
grain. The five species of grain, which weaken the soil more than legumes.

but they calculate for him the place of the trees etc.. They calculate the amount of crop that would have grown had he sown in the area of the trees what he sowed in the rest of the field, and he takes his proportionate share from the field's owner.
they came up in a place that is not fit for sowing, they calculate nothing for him. For he would not have sown in that area.

and if he took it as a sharecropper for seven years or more, he has the beams of the sycamore and the like. And he cuts the branches in its seventh year, since when he leaves the field they will return to what they were when he entered it.
his time has come to leave the field. The end of the sharecropping period they agreed upon.
that have not yet reached the point of being sold. That need more time in the ground to grow and become fit for sale.
they appraise them. They estimate their value, and the landowner pays the sharecropper his proportionate share.
so they divide the straw and the stubble. The leftovers of the crop.
the vine shoots. The branches of the vine that were pruned to improve the vine.
the reeds that are placed under the vines. Reeds whose purpose is to support the vine branches.
the beams of the sycamore and the like. Trees whose branches serve as building beams, and only after seven years do the cut branches become fit again to serve as beams.
one who takes a field from his fellow to plant. A sharecropper whose job is to plant saplings in the field.

the field's owner bears ten barren ones per se'ah. When he takes seeds sown densely in a nursery over an area of a beit se'ah and sows them over the area of the field, the field's owner bears the loss of up to ten barren saplings only (Tosefta Kifshuta, Bava Metzia p. 289; and see further explanations in Maggid Mishneh).
beyond this, they roll it all onto him. If there are more than ten barren saplings among those he took from a beit se'ah, the sharecropper must replace all the barren ones.
and it did not yield. It did not produce as it should.

for so he writes to the landowner... "and I will set up a pile before you". Since he undertook to set up a pile of grain ("kri"), and the measure of a pile of grain is two se'ah after deducting expenses, the sharecropper must fulfill the agreement even if he does not want to (see Bavli Bava Metzia 105a).
and I will plow. And I will till.
he let it lie fallow. He left it fallow, without working it.
as it would have yielded well. As it would have yielded had it been properly worked.

and why is he obligated to pay. For a monetary obligation that depends on a condition, that something may or may not happen, is not binding in terms of acquisition, since the obligated party always doubts whether the condition will be fulfilled and does not make a firm decision to transfer ownership even if it is fulfilled ("asmakhta" - see Hilchot Mekhirah 11:2).

because he did not stipulate a fixed amount upon himself etc.. Had he obligated himself to a sum fixed in advance and not according to the loss, it would have been an asmakhta, but when he obligated himself to pay what he caused to be lost, it is not an asmakhta (compare below 10:6).
I will give to it. I will give for the field (and in other manuscripts the reading is "I will give you," referring to the landowner).
one who takes a field to sow it with sesame and sowed it with wheat. The sesame crop is worth more, but it also weakens the soil more than wheat.

he has against him only a complaint. For the sharecropper deviated from what was agreed. But he cannot sue him for payment, since the value of the wheat is the same as the crop that should have grown from the sesame. And the sharecropper cannot deduct from the field owner's share the gain from having avoided weakening the soil (see Bavli Bava Metzia 104b).
according to what it should have yielded of sesame. According to the value of the sesame crop that should have grown there, since the sharecropper deviated without the field owner's consent.
they divide according to what they stipulated between them. The sharecropper gives the field's owner according to the ratio they set in advance.
even though the landowner profits. Because the profit is to be attributed not only to the sharecropper's work but also to the field owner's land.
and he said to them. After hiring them.
to start early and finish late. To work from sunrise until after sunset.
he cannot compel them. He cannot force them to add to the working hours beyond what is customary.
to feed. To provide the workers with food during work.

to provide dates or dried figs etc.. If the custom is to give them something additional to the basic food, for dessert and the like, he is obligated to give it (see Rabbenu Baruch, Bava Metzia 83a). Some explain that this refers to a place where it is customary to feed them only these items, so he is obligated only according to the custom (Meiri there).
dried figs. Dried figs.
and he said to him, "like one or two of the townspeople". That the wages will be determined accordingly.
they look at the lowest wage and the highest wage and assess between them. They check the lowest and the highest wage paid to a worker in the city, and he pays him the average between them.
he gives them four etc.. Since he took it upon himself to pay their wages, he pays as agreed, and takes from the householder only what the householder agreed to pay for the work.

according to the law of the country. According to the local custom. If the custom is to pay four, the householder pays them four; if the custom is three, the householder gives them three, and the workers cannot demand that the agent give them the extra one. The reason for the law is that when the agent deviated from the householder's words, the agency was voided, and it is considered as if the workers did work for the householder on their own initiative; and one who does work for another without his knowledge receives from him payment according to what is customarily given for the work (as below 9:9).
he gives them only three. For the householder's intention was to hire them for three, and there are some in the country who are hired for three, so he is not obligated to give them more.
when their work is not recognizable. That the value of the work cannot be assessed, for example if he hired them to dig and the pit has already filled with water (Bavli Bava Metzia 76a).
for had he not told them etc.. And since they toiled more, they take according to the value of their work.
at four each. Four for each worker.
even though their work is worth four. For their work is recognizable and this is its value.
and they have a complaint against the agent. For preventing them from earning four, but they cannot sue him for money.
they intended only that the householder would give more than four. But it is clear that they did not intend to agree to earn less than four.

if it is worth four they take four from the householder. As in the law of one who says to workers, "Your wages are on the householder," and they did recognizable work, that the householder gives them the value of their work (but if the agent said, "Your wages are on me," the agent pays the difference from his own pocket - Maggid Mishneh).

for they heard three and accepted it upon themselves. And even though they said "as the householder said," they may have meant that they trust that this is what the householder said, and not to stipulate that they take four if that is what the householder said.
and they misled the householder. That they did not come to do the work for which he hired them.
or the householder misled them. That before they came to the work the householder told them that he did not need their work.

they have against each other only a complaint. The workers must make the effort to find another employer, or the householder must make the effort to find other workers, but neither has a monetary claim against the other.
In what case is this said. That the workers have only a complaint against the householder.
that they did not go. To do the work.
but if they went etc.. The workers' going to the work is the beginning of the hiring, and therefore in certain cases the householder must pay, as follows.
the donkey drivers. Those who transport loads with donkeys.
and they did not find grain. That they were supposed to transport for him.
and they found the field wet. Soaked, so that it could not be worked.
if the householder inspected his work from the evening. He checked the evening before and saw that he needs the work.
the workers have nothing; what could he do. For he did what he was required to do, and had no way of knowing that the field would not need the work and of informing them.
and if he did not inspect, he gives them their wages. For he was obligated to check in order to spare them the loss involved in going.
like an idle worker. They calculate how much a worker would be willing to reduce from his wages in order to sit idle without the toil of work.
In what case is this said. That the householder has only a complaint against the workers.

and not slaves to slaves. From this verse the Sages learned that a Jew is not absolutely subjugated to the householder and may retract. Yet although he may retract, the householder may deduct from his wages or sue him for money if he caused him a loss, as explained below.
and what is the law of the worker etc.. One who receives wages for a day's work.

they appraise what he did and he takes. If the worker retracted in the middle of the day, he receives wages in proportion to the hours he worked, even if the second worker whom the householder will have to hire demands higher wages for the remaining hours.
and if he is a contractor. A worker who is not paid by the day but receives a lump sum for performing a defined task.

they appraise what he is yet to do. Unlike a worker, who in any case receives wages for the hours he worked, the contractor's pay is calculated in relation to what the householder will have to spend to hire a second contractor. Therefore if the second contractor whom the householder must hire asks for higher pay, the householder deducts the difference from the first contractor's pay (the reason for the distinction is that the contractor's pay is for a complete task, while a worker's pay is for his hours of work - Even ha-Azel, Mekhirah 13:18).

whether they cheapened it for him when he hired them. That the contractor demanded a low price for his work, and for another contractor the householder will have to pay a higher price, he deducts from his pay.

or whether the work became cheaper afterward. That the going rate in the country for this kind of contract work dropped, and the householder will pay less for the second contractor he hires, they assess how much it will cost to complete the work now, and the first contractor does not receive the difference (as below; and see Mirkevet ha-Mishneh, who explained differently based on the Gemara, and according to both explanations the phrase "what he is yet to do" is not clear, and this requires further study).
standing grain. Ripe grain standing ready for harvest.
for two sela'im. Which are eight dinars.

if it was worth six dinars. For example, if the work became more expensive and instead of eight dinars it is worth twelve, so that for the half of the work not done the householder must pay another contractor six dinars.

he gives them a shekel. Which is two dinars. Although by their original agreement he should have given them four dinars for half the work, since the work became more expensive and to finish it six dinars are now needed, he deducts this sum from their pay and gives them the remaining two dinars.
and if the remainder was worth two dinars. That the work became cheaper, and for the remaining half the householder will have to pay another contractor two dinars.
he gives them only a sela. Four dinars, the original value of half the work.

for they did only half the work. Although to complete the work the householder needs only two dinars, the contractor does not receive the two dinars left over from the pay for the remaining half, since he did not work for them.
In what case is this said. That the worker or contractor may retract.
in something that does not perish. Work that is not spoiled by their retracting.
his flax to be taken up from the soaking. To take the flax out of the water in which it is soaked, for if it is not taken out it will be spoiled and lost.
flutes for the dead or for the bride. For the eulogy or for the joy of a bride and groom, and they must be brought on time.
he may hire others against them or mislead them. As explained shortly.
"Come and take two". He may mislead them and promise them double wages so that they finish the work.
and he gives them only what he stipulated at first. He pays them only a sela, as he set for them at the outset.
he recovers the addition from them. Even though he already paid double wages, he can claim from them that they return the addition to him.

up to the wages of the first ones. That he pays the second workers out of the first workers' wages up to the full wage that he was supposed to pay them. For example, if he hired the first for two dinars a day and they retracted in the middle of the day, he pays the other workers up to two dinars for the half day that remained.
and if they had money in his hands. Money belonging to the workers is in the householder's possession.
the wages of the worker. The usual payment for a day's work.
In what case is this said. That the householder may hire others against them or mislead them.
but if there are workers there to hire for their wages. If the householder can find workers who will complete the work for the same wages he would have paid the first workers to complete it.
and they appraise for the hired worker what he did, and for the contractor what he is yet to do. Even though this is a perishable matter, the law is the law of a worker who retracted with permission.
and was seized. Was taken against his will.

he may not say to him, "Here is yours before you" etc.. The worker cannot say, "Here is yours before you," and claim that the employer's luck caused it and that he must pay him his full wages; rather, he pays him only for what he managed to work before he was taken (unlike the law of an animal taken for the king's service, where the lessor can make this claim, as above 5:1; for the reason for the distinction see Mirkevet ha-Mishneh).
and the river stopped in the middle of the day. The river from which they irrigate stopped flowing, and they cannot irrigate the field from it.

they have only the wages for what they did. And the householder is exempt from paying them for the rest of the day, since this is not common and the householder did not know beforehand so as to inform the workers.
for the workers knew the way of this river. And on that understanding they were hired for this work.
strangers. They are not from the place, and do not know the ways of the river.

he gives them the wages for the whole day because he should have informed them. Since he knows about this and they do not, he should have told them in advance that they would not receive pay for a full day's work, and he must pay them their wages.
and rain came and watered it. After they began to irrigate, rain fell.
they have only what they did. Since the householder did not know about this beforehand, he pays them only for the work they did before the rain came.

the river came and watered it, he gives them all their wages. If the river rose to the channels made for irrigating the field and the workers did not have to toil much in irrigating, he pays them full wages for their work, for Heaven eased their work by the rising of the river (unlike rainfall, in which they did not toil at all - Maggid Mishneh; and see Mirkevet ha-Mishneh and Or Sameach, who brought further explanations of the difference between rainfall and the rising of the river; and see also Lechem Mishneh, who explained that he does not pay them full wages but as idle workers).
for a sharecropper is like a partner, not like a worker. And his payment depends on the yield of the field, regardless of his toil in working it.
and the work was completed in the middle of the day. The work for which the worker was hired was completed.
if he has other work like it or lighter than it etc.. But the householder cannot demand that the worker do work harder than the work for which he was hired.
and if he has nothing for him to do. He has no work like it or lighter for him to do.

he gives him his wages as an idle worker. Since he hired him for the whole day. And for the time in which he did no actual work, he pays him as much as a person wants to earn while sitting idle and not toiling at work.
villagers. People of a village.

whose way is to toil much and if he does not occupy himself with work he will fall ill. Such workers are used to hard, continuous work, and idleness is hard for them and gives them no pleasure but distress.
he gives him his full wages. For he went and returned as the householder required of him, and the fact that he brought nothing does not depend on him but on the householder.
he may not say to him, "Take what you brought as your wages". That he take the fruit as payment for his errand.
rather he gives him all his wages. Because the messenger carried out his errand.
and showed him that of his fellow. Supplied him with work belonging to another person.
and he takes from his fellow the benefit he derived from this work. Even if he hired the worker at a higher price, his fellow pays him only according to the value of the benefit at the going rate.
to work with him in straw and stubble. To gather straw and stubble in his field.
"Take what you did as your wages". After he worked, he told him to take the straw and stubble in place of payment in money.
