we do not listen to him. Even if it is worth the same as the wages, the householder must pay the worker in money, since the worker was hired on that understanding and expects payment in money.
and if after he accepted it etc.. If the worker agreed to take the straw and stubble in place of money, and the householder wants to retract and take the grain and pay money, he cannot retract.
what a worker finds belongs to himself. A worker who found a lost item during his work, the find belongs to him and not to the householder.

even though he said to him, "Work with me today" etc.. Even if he did not hire him for a particular task, we do not say that his find belongs to the householder, and all the more so when he hired him for a particular task, since the find is not part of the particular task.
for the river receded. The water level of the river dropped and pools of water containing fish were formed.
his finds belong to the householder, even if he found a purse full of dinars. Since the essence of his hiring is to gather finds, even if he found other finds, they belong to the householder.
One who lends to his fellow against a pledge. A lender who received a pledge from the borrower as security for the loan.
he is a paid guardian. Because he benefits from the pledge's being bound to the loan (Rabbi Yosef ibn Migash, Shevuot 43b).
an armed robber. An armed bandit.
he swears that it was an accident. As is the law of a paid guardian (as above 1:2).
"Guard for me and I will guard for you". That each guards the other's item, in return for the other guarding his item. And they accept the guarding upon themselves at the same time.

this is guarding in the presence of the owners. For at the time of receiving the deposit, each of them took upon himself the task of guarding the item for the other, and a guardian who borrowed or hired the owners together with their deposit is exempt even if the item was lost through negligence (see above 1:3).

he said to him, "Guard for me today and I will guard for you tomorrow" etc.. Since the owners are not engaged in guarding for the guardian at the time he begins guarding the item for them, this is not guarding in the presence of the owners, and each of them is considered a paid guardian.

all of them became paid guardians for one another. And even a borrower, who is generally liable for accidents because he benefits without payment, in this case has the law of a paid guardian, who is exempt for accidents, since in return for the borrowing he guards for his fellow or lends to him.
all craftsmen. Artisans who take the owners' raw materials to their homes in order to make items from them or to process them for them.

paid guardians. Although they do not receive payment for guarding the item, they receive payment for their work and benefit from holding the item with them, and therefore they are classified as paid guardians.
the craftsman is an unpaid guardian. For when the craftsman has finished his work, he is no longer considered as deriving benefit from holding the item.

"Bring money and take yours" etc.. Since he put the bringing of money before giving the item to its owner, it implies that he is holding the item as a pledge that he will pay him, and this benefit classifies him as a paid guardian.
to the carpenter. A woodworker.
a shiddah. A kind of low chest with legs.
a teivah. A stationary chest.
and a migdal. A wall cabinet.

for the craftsman does not acquire the improvement of the item. When the craftsman received raw materials and made an item from them, although the increase in the item's value came from the craftsman's action, the improvement does not belong to him but to the owners. Therefore if he broke the item he made, he must pay the owners the value of the item and not the value of the raw materials.
and the pot scorched it. He boiled too much the pot in which he cooks the wool with the dye, and the wool burned and was ruined.
its dye was ugly. That the dye did not take well and its appearance is not nice, even if it is the shade he requested (Perush ha-Mishnayot, Bava Kamma 9:4).

if the improvement exceeds the expense etc.. Because the craftsman deviated from the owner's wishes, the owner of the item does not pay him his wages. But to prevent a loss to the craftsman, the Sages ordained that the craftsman's hand be on the bottom, and the owner of the item pays him the lower of the expense or the improvement. For example, if the garment was worth a dinar before dyeing and a dinar and a half after dyeing, and the dyer's expenses were a quarter dinar, he pays him a quarter dinar and no more. And if the dyer's expenses were three quarters of a dinar, he pays him half a dinar, which is the value of the improvement alone (there).
"I do not want this ordinance". That he does not want to take the item and pay the improvement or the expense, but wants to receive the value of the raw materials he gave.
we do not listen to him. If the craftsman does not agree to this, since this ordinance is also for the craftsman's benefit (see Perush ha-Mishnayot there).

we do not listen to him, for the craftsman does not acquire the improvement of an item he made. And he cannot claim that because of his work the item now belongs to him, since the improvement belongs to the owner of the item and not to the craftsman.

and not to soak them and made them coarse flour or bran. The miller did not wet them with water before grinding as he should have done so that the grinding would come out well, and instead of fine, sifted flour, the flour came out coarse and poor.
to the baker. A baker.
crumbling bread. Bread that was not baked enough, so when it is taken it breaks and falls apart.
to the butcher. To the slaughterer.
and made it nevelah. He made it a nevelah (improperly slaughtered carcass) by his slaughtering.

because they are paid bailees. Like all craftsmen who receive payment for their work. And a paid guardian is exempt only for a major accident, and these cases are not defined as a major accident, since the craftsman was required to be careful in his work.

if the butcher was expert and slaughtered for free, he is exempt from paying. When he slaughtered for free he has the law of an unpaid guardian, who is liable only for negligence. And since the butcher is an expert, the mishap that occurred is not considered negligence, and he is exempt for it.
and if he is not expert, even though it is for free, he must pay. Since he is not expert, the mishap is considered negligence, for which an unpaid guardian is liable.
one who shows a dinar to a money changer. Shows a coin to a money changer who breaks coins, to determine whether the coin is good, and if so they will accept it from his fellow.
and it was found to be bad. It became clear that it cannot be used in trade.
if he showed it for payment, he must pay. For he has the law of a paid guardian, similar to the law of the craftsmen mentioned.

and this is provided that he says to the money changer etc.. A money changer who is not expert is liable only if the owner of the coin said to him explicitly that he relies on him, or if it was evident that he relies on him even if he did not say so explicitly.
it is upon them to bring proof that they are experts. In order to be exempt from payment in cases where they acted for free.
that the one who plants trees takes half of the improvement and the landowner half. The contractor plants and tends the saplings for the field owner and shares the profits equally with him.
and he planted and it improved, and he planted and it was lost. Some of what he planted bore fruit and improved, and some did not bear fruit and was lost, and the gain is greater than the loss.

they calculate for him half the improvement that is his and deduct from it what he lost. They deduct from his share of the profit of the saplings that did well the loss of the saplings that did not do well, so that the field's owner receives half of the profit that would have come from the saplings had they all done well.
and even if he stipulated upon himself that if he lost he would take nothing. The planter stipulated that if the saplings did not do well he would take nothing for his share.

this is an asmakhta. An obligation that has no validity and need not be fulfilled because it is conditioned on a future event (but in the first case it is not considered an asmakhta, since the loss he caused is deducted from him - compare above 8:13).
and so was their custom, that the sharecropper takes a third. Likewise they were accustomed in that place that a sharecropper working a planted field gets a third of the crop.
and he wanted to withdraw. To leave his contract voluntarily.
he must bring down a sharecropper for it. Who will tend the saplings in the planter's place.
and the landowner takes his half. As he was to receive originally.

and the sharecropper takes a third, and the remaining sixth belongs to the planter. They pay the sharecropper a third out of the half that the planter was to receive, and the remaining sixth ("shetut") is given to the planter. For example, if the crop was worth twelve dinars: the field's owner takes six dinars, the sharecropper takes four dinars, which is a third of the total crop, and the planter takes two dinars, which is a sixth of the total crop.
for he removed himself willingly. The planter wanted to withdraw, and therefore what the sharecropper receives is deducted from his share.

one who plants trees for the townspeople and lost. Who was appointed by the townspeople to engage in planting and his saplings did not grow properly, so he lost the saplings and also the profit of the fruit the saplings were supposed to yield.

and likewise the butcher of the townspeople who made the animals nevelot. A slaughterer appointed by the townspeople, and the animals often become nevelot through his slaughtering. Although he pays the value of the animal, sometimes a person needs meat to serve his guests, and when he cannot find another animal he is embarrassed, and sometimes much meat is needed and because of the slaughterer it is not available (Maggid Mishneh).
and the one who lets blood. For medical treatment.
who injured. Who caused injury in the course of his work.
and the scribe who erred in documents. Who wrote documents inaccurately and caused a monetary loss.
and did not teach. And the students were kept from their studies.
taught erroneously. Taught in a faulty way, and an error absorbed by children becomes fixed and hard to correct.
they remove them. From their appointment.

because they are as if forewarned, and they stand until they take care in their work. They are warned in advance to be careful in their work, so there is no need to warn them again before removing them.
and if he delayed beyond its time. Even though he intends to pay him.
and the sun shall not set upon it. He may not wait to pay the hired worker's wages until after sunset (for a night worker - as below).
and one is not flogged for this prohibition, since he must pay. And any prohibition that carries a monetary obligation is not punishable by flogging (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2).
both the rental fee for an animal and the rental fee for vessels. Payment for renting an animal or vessels.
and a ger toshav. A non-Jew who lives in the Land and accepted upon himself to keep the seven Noahide commandments.

and if another, he does not transgress a negative commandment concerning him. For regarding the negative commandment it says, "You shall not oppress your neighbor... the wages of a hired worker shall not remain with you overnight" (Leviticus 19:13), and the Sages expounded that a non-Jew, who is not called "your neighbor," is not transgressed against by this prohibition (Bavli Bava Metzia 111b).
one who withholds a hired worker's wages. Who does not intend to pay him at all.

"You shall not oppress". This prohibition includes two verses: "You shall not oppress a hired worker" (Deuteronomy 24:14) and "You shall not oppress your neighbor" (Leviticus 19:13), and they are counted as one prohibition (Lechem Mishneh).
and because of "you shall not rob". For when he refuses to pay him what is due him he also transgresses the prohibition "and you shall not rob" (Leviticus 19:13).

and because of "it shall not remain overnight" and because of "and the sun shall not set upon it". Although the first verse was said of a day worker and the second of a night worker, one who withholds a hired worker's wages and does not intend to pay him transgresses each of them when its time comes, even if it is a day worker alone or a night worker alone (Kesef Mishneh).
a day worker collects all night. For a worker who works all day and finishes his work at sunset, the employer is commanded to pay him during the night until dawn.
and a night worker collects all day. For a worker who works all night and finishes his work at daybreak, the employer is commanded to pay him during the day until sunset.
and an hourly day worker collects all day. For a worker who works a few hours in the day and finishes his work before sunset, the employer is commanded to pay him until sunset.
a weekly worker. Whom he hired for a week.
a worker for a shavua. Whom he hired for seven years.
he left during the day. He finished his work in the daytime.
he gave his cloak to the craftsman. To repair it, and he is not a day worker but is paid as a contractor.
even if he delayed ten days, he does not transgress. Even if he delayed paying because he took the cloak later, and paid when he took it, he does not transgress the prohibition of delaying wages.
he gave it to him in the middle of the day. The craftsman returned the cloak to its owner in the middle of the day.

he transgresses "it shall not remain overnight". Here the intent is the prohibition of delaying wages in general (compare the wording below 5:4). If he returned it to him during the day and did not pay him until sunset, he transgresses "and the sun shall not set upon it," and if he returned it at night and did not pay until morning, he transgresses "it shall not remain overnight" (Sma 339:11).
if he said to them. The agent to the workers.

this one because he did not hire them. The householder does not transgress because he did not hire them directly. Some explained that the reason is that the workers take into account the possibility that the householder will not pay them on time (Tosafot Rid, Bava Metzia 111a).
and this one because their work is not with him. The agent does not transgress because they are not working for him, and paying their wages is not his obligation.

and if he did not say to them, "Your wages are on the householder," the agent transgresses. For when the agent hires without specification, payment of the wages is his responsibility and he transgresses "it shall not remain overnight."
but if he did not demand it of him. So it turns out that the delay of the wages is with the worker's consent.

or he assigned him to another and he accepted. The employer instructed another to pay the worker for his work and the worker agreed to this (some explain that "accepted" means that the person who was asked to pay agreed to it - see Kesef Mishneh).
he is exempt. He does not transgress the prohibition of delaying wages, but he must pay him his wages.

even though he already transgressed a positive and negative commandment. When the day passed in the case of a night worker, or the night passed in the case of a day worker, he transgressed a Torah prohibition, and from then on he does not transgress a Torah prohibition at each moment.
and every time that he delays he transgresses a prohibition of their words. He transgresses a rabbinic prohibition based on the verse in Proverbs.

the Sages ordained that he swears while holding a sacred object, like any who swears and collects etc.. The Sages ordained that in certain cases where there is no Torah-law obligation of an oath, the claimant may swear on his claim and collect from the defendant (although generally the defendant swears to be exempt from the claim against him), and this oath is taken while the swearer holds a Torah scroll (see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:2).

because the householder is preoccupied with his workers. The householder is preoccupied with his business and accounts and may think he paid although he did not, whereas the worker, since he awaits payment, remembers well and the matter is clearer to him.

even if the employer was a minor, the worker swears and collects. In matters from which a minor benefits, the Sages ordained that one may sue him. And since a minor benefits from having workers hired for him, the worker who claimed swears and collects (there 5:11).

since he could have said, "There were never any dealings" etc.. Since he could have exempted himself by claiming that he did not hire him, he is believed to claim that he paid and to be exempt from the oath of the worker who swears and collects ("migo").

and the householder swears a hesset oath that he paid. In a case where the householder denies the entire claim, for example claiming that he paid all the wages, he swears a rabbinic oath without holding a sacred object, like any who denies everything (see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:3).
or a Torah oath if he admitted to part. For one who admits to part of the claim is obligated a Torah oath (there, halachot 1-2).

if he had one witness that he hired him, it is of no avail. For the Sages ordained that the worker swears only where there are two witnesses, not one witness whose testimony is not strong (Maggid Mishneh).
and likewise if he sued him after his time. A day worker who sued after the night passed, and a night worker who sued after the day passed.

even though he hired him with witnesses, the one who seeks to collect from his fellow bears the burden of proof. For the householder is not suspected of transgressing the prohibition of delaying wages, and in addition, the worker does not leave his wages in the householder's hands without a claim (see Bavli Bava Metzia 113a).

if he brought proof that he claimed it throughout its time, he swears and collects for that entire day of claim. When the worker brings proof that he demanded his wages within their time and the householder postponed payment, the worker may swear for the entire twenty-four hours of the claim, that is, the morning or night in which he claimed from the householder and the night or morning after it, as explained in the next paragraph (Taz and Gra on Shulchan Aruch, Choshen Mishpat 89:3; and see Sma there and Yad Pashut, who explained differently).

its time is all of the third night, and on the third day he does not swear and collect. The time for claiming is on the third night, and if he did not claim, he cannot swear and collect on the third day.
but from the fourth night onward, the one who seeks to collect from his fellow bears the burden of proof. For he stopped and did not claim on the third day.
and likewise if he brought witnesses that he was claiming continuously until Thursday. That he continued to claim throughout day and night until the beginning of Thursday night.

the Sages did not ordain that the worker swears. The Sages ordained that a worker swears and collects only regarding the payment itself, not regarding the amount of the wages, because the householder remembers the amount he set with the workers (Rabbi Yosef ibn Migash, Shevuot 46a).
even though he already gave him the two. And he denies the remaining dinar.

or he said to him, "Here you are". Even if he has not yet paid, if the householder offers the worker the two that he admits to and says to him "here," he is not considered as admitting to part regarding the additional dinar but as denying everything (Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:3).

the householder swears while holding a sacred object. By strict law in these cases, where the defendant denies everything, there is only an obligation to swear a hesset oath without holding a sacred object (there 5:4), but regarding a hired worker the Sages ordained that the householder swears while holding a sacred object.
In what case is this said. That the Sages ordained that the householder swears while holding a sacred object in order to be exempt.

but if he hired him without witnesses or he sued him after his time, the householder swears a hesset oath. For even in a case of a claim for the whole wage where the worker swears and collects, the Sages made their ordinance conditional on his having hired him with witnesses and claimed within its time; all the more so in a case of a claim about the amount of the wages, the Sages' ordinance that the householder swears while holding a sacred object is conditional on this; therefore he swears a hesset oath without holding a sacred object.
one who gives his cloak to a craftsman. So that he will repair it for him.

if he can claim that it was bought and is in his hands etc.. For example, if it is with him and they did not see it in his possession, so that he could have claimed that he bought it, and on this basis his claim about the amount of payment is also accepted (see also Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 9:2).
and if the cloak left his possession or he has no presumption of ownership in it etc.. If he returned it or they saw it in his hand, so that he cannot claim that he bought it.

the owner of the cloak swears a hesset oath... for this is not like the law of the hired worker. For with a hired worker the Sages ordained that the householder swear a severe oath while holding a sacred object, so that the worker not go away broken-hearted, since he stakes his life on receiving his wages for his livelihood; but with a craftsman, whose livelihood does not depend on daily wages like a hired worker, the owner of the item swears only a hesset oath (Beit Yosef, Choshen Mishpat 89; Mirkevet ha-Mishneh).

they do not burden him and do not roll over onto him at all. Generally a person who is obligated to swear on one claim can be made to swear on other claims together with this oath ("gilgul shevuah"), but with a hired worker the householder who administers the oath may not do so, so that the worker will not avoid swearing and go away broken-hearted (Meiri, Shevuot 49a).

for they are lenient with him and open for him first etc.. If the worker does not know about the possibility of swearing, the court must inform him of it, and even encourage him to swear if he is hesitant.
with an oath like that of the Torah. While holding a Torah scroll.

and its work was not yet completed. For maaser (tithe), for after its work for maaser has been completed the worker may not eat, whether detached or attached (completion of work is a term for the final operations in processing the crop, and it is the stage at which the produce becomes fully obligated in terumot and ma'asrot - see Hilchot Ma'aser 3:1-2).

whether attached, and their actions are the completion of the work etc.. For with attached produce the worker may eat from the grain only in the final stage of the work he was hired to do (as below 12:2).
When you come into your neighbor's vineyard. And the verse continues: "you may eat grapes as you wish, until you are satisfied, but you shall not put any in your vessel."
When you come into your neighbor's standing grain. And the verse continues: "you may pluck ears with your hand, but you shall not put a sickle to your neighbor's standing grain."
from oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in explaining the verses.
for had he not hired him etc.. For surely the verse is not speaking of a person who went down into his fellow's vineyard without permission.

for one who works with detached produce eats of something whose work has not been completed for maaser and for challah. The worker may eat throughout his work as long as the crop's work has not been completed with regard to the obligation of maaser (tithe) or challah (in the case of items that were tithed and are destined to be made into bread - see below 5:5).
he eats only when he finishes a task. He may not eat during his work, but only after completing a full unit of work.

for example, when he harvests and puts into the basket until he fills it etc.. The work of harvesting is to fill baskets with grapes, and after filling, the basket's contents are emptied into the place where the harvested grapes are gathered; the filling of each basket counts as a separate unit of work.
he eats only after he has filled the basket. Only after filling each basket is he permitted by the Torah to eat.
but because of the duty to return a lost item to its owners. To spare the householder the loss involved in the worker's interrupting his work while eating.
from row to row. From one row of the vineyard to another.
and on their return from the winepress. After emptying the grapes there and returning to the vineyard to continue harvesting.

one who interrupts his work and eats, or who ate not at the time of completing the work. For example, he stopped in the middle of filling the basket in order to eat, even if he ate while filling and not after the filling was completed.
for as long as he is engaged in reaping he may not swing the sickle for his own eating. While swinging the sickle for the householder, he may not swing it for his own eating.
who carried away in his hand some of what he harvested. Took some of the grain for himself to eat at another time.

and one is not flogged for these two prohibitions, since if he ate or carried away he must pay. And any prohibition that carries a monetary obligation is not punishable by flogging (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2).
and one who churns. Produces butter from milk.
and one who makes cheese. Prepares cheese.
does not eat. The worker may not eat during the work.

even though he pulls out small ones from among large ones etc.. Although part of the weeding process is pulling out small onions or garlic from among the large ones to allow the large ones to grow well, pulling the small ones is not considered completion of the work, because the purpose of the work is pulling the large ones.
and needless to say, guards of gardens and orchards etc.. For guarding is not defined as work (below 5:9).
such as cucumber and gourd fields. Plots of cucumbers and gourds.
who do not eat at all. Unlike guards of detached grain, who may eat by local custom (as below 5:9).
and one who shapes. Shapes loaves from the dough.
because their work has been completed for challah. For from the time the flour and water are mixed and turned into dough ("rolling"), it is obligated in challah (Hilchot Bikkurim 8:4).
one who separates dates and dried figs. A worker who separates dates or dried figs that stuck together.
because their work has been completed for maaser. And one who works with detached produce does not eat after the work has been completed for the obligation of maaser and challah (above 5:2).
for example, he hired them to pick out pebbles. He hired the workers to pick out dirt and small stones from the wheat.

for their work has not yet been completed for challah. And with grain that has a further obligation after the obligation of tithes, the workers may eat from it until it becomes subject to its last obligation.
to sift. To sift.

its rounds came apart. Figs that were pressed into a round cake and then came apart; they had already become obligated in maaser from when he smoothed the cake and made it nice (Hilchot Ma'aser 3:16), and now he hires the workers to make a new round.

and its barrels were opened. Their work had already been completed for maaser from when the wine was put into barrels (there, halachah 14), and now what was in them was poured back into the wine pit, and he hired the workers to return the wine to the barrels.

and its gourds were cut. The meaning of this case is not entirely clear, and with some difficulty one can explain that the householder had gourds that he set in a pile, and thereby their work was completed for maaser (see Hilchot Ma'aser 3:8), and afterward the gourds were cut up and scattered, and the householder hired workers to gather them back into a pile (it should be noted that this halachah is based on the Mishnah in Bava Metzia 7:7, and these words are not found in most versions of the Mishnah there nor in Rambam's text of the Mishnah).

and if he did not inform them, he tithes and feeds them. In all these cases the workers had no way of knowing that their work had already been completed for maaser, and they were hired on the assumption that they may eat; therefore if the householder did not inform them of this beforehand, he must tithe the produce and wine and let them eat of it.
in your neighbor's vineyard. And hekdesh (consecrated property) is not included in "your neighbor."

to make into his neta revai, these may not eat. The fruit of a tree in its fourth year is called "neta revai" and must be brought up to Jerusalem and eaten there, or redeemed with money and food bought with it in Jerusalem, whereupon the fruit itself becomes permitted to eat (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 9:4); therefore the workers may not eat of it.

and if he did not inform them, he redeems and feeds them. If the householder did not inform the workers of this, they were hired on the assumption that they may eat, and the householder must redeem the fruit and let the workers eat of it.
and all similar kinds of work. That are at the stage of completion of work.
winepresses. The place where grapes are trodden to produce wine, where there is a yield of grapes or wine.
and piles. Of grain and the like.

eat by local custom, since a guard is not like one who does work. By strict law a guard is not considered a worker, since he does not do any action on the grain itself. But it became the custom in the countries to allow him to eat like a worker, and this custom is a sort of rabbinic ordinance (Meiri, Bava Metzia 93a).
but if he worked with one of his limbs etc.. Any act of work of any kind classifies him as a worker who eats by Torah law.
and one who works with this vine does not eat from another vine. He may eat only from the same tree in which he is working.
and if he stipulated with the householder the amount he will eat. If he agreed in advance with the householder how much he would eat, he may eat that amount in any manner he wishes.
to suck. To suck.
his children and his wife. For the worker himself certainly may not interrupt his work for this.
they scorch the ears of grain for him in fire. They singe the ears to roast the kernels and improve their taste.
gluttonous eating. Eating more than satiety.
and he is permitted to hold himself back until the place of the good ones and eat. He can wait before eating until his work reaches a better crop.
and he may. He is permitted.
a cucumber. A cucumber.
and dates. Dates.
even though he hired him for a ma'ah of silver. Which is a sixth of a dinar, so that he eats more than his wages.
as it says, "as much as you desire, to your fill". And the Sages learned that the amount the Torah permitted for eating depends on the worker's satiety.
and he will be closing the door in his own face. For if he behaves this way, field owners will refrain from hiring him for work.

he was guarding four or five piles. That belong to different people. Some explain that this refers to a case where they belong to one person, and so that his damage not be noticeable (Meiri, Bava Metzia 93a).
proportionally. That he eats an equal amount from each of the piles, or perhaps it means in proportion to the size of the pile.
workers who have not gone warp and woof etc.. Workers treading grapes drink from the juice only after they have walked from side to side along the length and width of the winepress.
for they are still working only with grapes. Like a worker harvesting grapes who may not eat from the figs.
the grape juice. The juice that comes out of the grapes.
"I will give a little of what I took to eat to my children and wife". Even if he already took the fruit in his hand.

for the Torah granted the right only to the worker himself. The worker's right by Torah law is only that he eat the fruit while working, and he has no monetary ownership of the fruit that would let him pass it on to others.
even a nazir. Who is forbidden to eat grapes, and cannot eat them during his work.
who was working, he and his wife and his children and his slaves. All of whom were hired together for work with the householder.

and he stipulated with the householder that they would not eat etc.. For example, they agreed that the worker would receive additional pay from the householder for this. And he may stipulate to waive the right the Torah granted him.

for they do not eat from their father's or their master's but from Heaven's. Therefore, although a person has a stake in what his household members who depend on his table acquire, here it is not a monetary right but a right to eat as part of the Torah's commandments, and it is necessary that they too waive their right toward the householder, and a minor cannot waive (see Hilchot Gezelah va-Avedah 15:16).
from its load. Burden, cargo.
until it is unloading. Until they unload from it what is on it.
provided that he does not take in his hand. The animal's owner may not feed it from the load.
and it was said "an ox while it threshes" only as the present case. Because it is the current and common situation.
and one who muzzles the worker. Who prevents him from eating during work as he is entitled to by law (as explained in the previous chapter).
is exempt. For the prohibition of muzzling applies to animals and not to people.
even if he muzzled it by voice, he is flogged. For example, he scolded it and startled it to prevent it from eating.
four kavs for a cow and three kavs for a donkey. This is the daily eating measure that the hirer is obligated to supply for these animals.

for from the time of pulling he became obligated for its food, and he is not liable to flogging until he threshes with it muzzled. Although one who does an act that carries flogging and is also obligated in payment for this act (such as one who cuts down his fellow's tree on a festival) has the law that he is flogged and does not pay, that is only when he became liable to flogging and payment at one time. But in this case, since the obligation to feed the animal, for which he pays the owner, already applied to him from the time of pulling (see Hilchot She'elah u-Fikadon 1:4), and the flogging obligation applies to him only from the time of threshing, he is flogged and pays (see Hilchot Genevah 3:1-2).
a Jew who threshes with a gentile's cow etc.. The prohibition depends on the one who threshes and not on the identity of the animal's owner.

he said to a gentile, "Muzzle my cow and thresh with it". He told a gentile to muzzle his cow, and then the gentile threshed the Jew's grain (see R. Y. Shilat in Rambam Meduyak; and Yad Pashut explained that he told the gentile to muzzle and the Jew threshed the grain, and he is not flogged for this because he did not perform the act of muzzling).
a thorn lodged in its mouth. A thorn entered its mouth on its own and prevents it from eating.
a lion crouched by it from outside. And out of fear it refrains from eating.
or its young crouched outside. And out of longing for its calf it does not eat.
it was thirsty and he does not give it to drink. And because of thirst it does not eat.

it is forbidden but he is not flogged. In all these cases the person caused indirectly that the animal be muzzled and not eat, or did not remove what bothers it and prevents it from eating; therefore it is prohibited but he is not flogged (see Yad Pashut).
let it be loosened. Let it drop.
because the road led them astray. They lost their way and in doing so walked on the grain.

he does not transgress concerning them the prohibition "do not muzzle". For a kohen may not feed terumah to a Jew's animal (see Hilchot Terumot 9:7), and this prohibition is not overridden by the prohibition "do not muzzle." And maaser sheni is not included in the verse "while it threshes" because it is the property of the Most High. Likewise, cows that strayed off the path are not included in "while it threshes," as this is not considered threshing (see Tosafot and Meiri on Bava Metzia 90a).
but because of appearances. So that it not look as if he is muzzling it and transgressing the prohibition (and with cows that strayed off the path there is no appearance problem).

he brings a little of that kind and hangs it for them in baskets. He brings chullin (ordinary) grain of the same type that the animal is threshing and puts a little in a bag-like pouch hung on the animal's neck so that it can eat (see the picture on the next page).

with maaser sheni of demai etc.. Terumot and ma'asrot separated from the grain of ignorant people, where it is not known whether it was tithed, and the Sages decreed that terumot and ma'asrot be separated from it out of doubt (see Hilchot Ma'aser 9:1-2).
and with the growth of terumah. Terumah that was sown in the ground, and the Sages decreed that what grows from it be forbidden like terumah (see Hilchot Terumot 11:21).

he transgresses "do not muzzle". Because by Torah law this grain is permitted to eat, and only the Sages decreed a prohibition on it, and a rabbinic decree does not override the prohibition "do not muzzle." And he hangs a pouch on the animal's neck and puts in it permitted grain of the same type, so that he is not muzzling the animal and not feeding it what the Sages forbade (see there, halachah 28).
the householder is permitted. Before he leases his cow to another.
and the hirer is permitted to feed it bundles of straw etc.. One who rents the cow may feed it bundles of straw before the threshing, so that it will eat less during the threshing.
so that they will not eat many grapes. While they do their work in the vineyard.

to dip their bread in tzir. A liquid exuded from pickled fish. This tzir cleans the intestines and enables one to eat more, and it cannot be drunk by itself, so bread is dipped in it (see Perush ha-Mishnayot, Berakhot 6:7). And it is permitted for workers to eat this tzir before they begin their work in the vineyard.

just as the householder is warned not to rob the wages of a poor man. The wages of a hired worker, for generally the poor hire themselves out for work, and so is the wording of the verse: "You shall not oppress a poor and needy hired worker" (Deuteronomy 24:14 and Ramban there).
and spends the entire day under a curse. He wastes his day in idleness and diminishes the householder's money (see Deuteronomy 28:20 and Rashi and Ibn Ezra there).

the Sages were so scrupulous about the fourth blessing of Birkat ha-Mazon that he should not say it. For the worker, during his work, is exempt from this blessing and shortens the second and third blessings because of interruption of work (see Hilchot Berakhot 2:2).
